stories.title: Russian attack kills 20 in a Ukrainian city as peace talks are held in Miami
summary: A Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia early on Saturday killed 20 people, including three children.
Officials said Russia hit several places at the same time, and part of an apartment building fell down.
At the same time, officials from the US, Ukraine and Europe met in Miami to discuss a plan to end the war.
US envoy Steve Witkoff called the talks constructive, and they covered energy, grain exports and security guarantees.
why: It was the third attack this week in which many civilians died, and the war is now in its fifth year.

stories.title: The US lets Russia sell diesel again to bring down high fuel prices
summary: US President Donald Trump has agreed a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel onto world markets.
Russia will first supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, then 500,000 tonnes in November and more later.
The US Treasury said it would give a temporary licence so that the fuel can be sold despite sanctions.
US diesel reached a record average price of $6.52 a gallon in September, as the war with Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz.
why: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a weak decision, and the EU said it was not the time to ease pressure on Russia.
Some experts say the amounts are small, because the US alone uses about 3.7 million barrels of diesel a day.

stories.title: Indian police detain more than 1,000 people to stop a protest in New Delhi
summary: Police in New Delhi detained more than 1,000 people on Saturday to stop a large protest against India's chief election official, Gyanesh Kumar.
The protest was called by youth groups, including the Cockroach Janta Party, whose founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken off a plane in Delhi.
Trains to the city were cancelled, mobile internet was switched off, and the main protest site was closed.
A spokesman for the governing BJP said the protest had failed and the country was calm.
why: The protesters say a review of voter lists removed many voters and helped the BJP win some state elections.
Amnesty International called for everyone detained for peaceful protest to be released.

stories.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea blame each other for starting a war
summary: Ethiopia has told the UN Security Council that Eritrea has carried out an all-out invasion of its northern Tigray region.
Ethiopia's foreign minister said Eritrean troops had moved up to 60 kilometres inside the country, and he asked for them to leave.
Eritrea rejected the claim and said Ethiopia had been fighting an unprovoked war against it for more than three years.
Eritrea also accused Ethiopia of wanting to take Assab, an Eritrean port on the Red Sea.
why: Ethiopia lost its coast when Eritrea became independent in 1993, and it has often said it needs access to the sea.
The two neighbours fought a border war from 1998, and they cut diplomatic ties in late September.

stories.title: Taiwan's president says more defence spending is meant to deter war
summary: Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te said in his National Day speech on Saturday that the island wants peace but will not give up its freedom.
He said higher defence spending is meant to deter a war, not to provoke one.
His government has planned a record 1.1 trillion Taiwan dollars, or about US$34.5 billion, for defence in 2027.
China's Taiwan Affairs Office criticised the speech and repeated that Taiwan is part of China.
why: China claims Taiwan, an island of 23 million people, and has not ruled out using force to take control of it.
The holiday marks 115 years since the 1911 uprising that ended China's last imperial dynasty.

stories.title: Report asks why Solomon Islands MPs get medical care overseas while patients wait
summary: An ABC investigation suggests some MPs in Solomon Islands received publicly funded medical treatment abroad when cheaper care was available at home.
In 2025 the prime minister's office spent about $1.5 million on overseas health care for MPs, while about $1.2 million was set aside for ordinary citizens.
Some doctors say they felt pressure from politicians to approve the trips, but the attorney-general said the system is legal.
Prime Minister Matthew Wale said that from next year all such funding will go through a commission with stricter rules.
why: Many citizens must wait or raise money themselves for surgery overseas, such as a young mother with heart disease who needs nearly $35,000.

stories.title: Billionaires and big countries race to the Moon, but who owns it?
summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin both have plans to build settlements on the Moon.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says no country can claim the Moon, and it must be used only for peaceful purposes.
However, the treaty says nothing about mining, and a 2015 US law lets American companies own and sell resources they take from space.
So far 76 countries have signed the Artemis Accords, which are led by NASA, but Russia and China have rejected them.
why: Experts say a new, more detailed agreement may be needed, as the UN expects the space industry could be worth a trillion dollars by 2030.

stories.title: High silver prices hurt the makers of traditional wedding shoes in India
summary: In Lucknow, in northern India, craftsmen have made silver wedding shoes called nagras by hand for about 400 years.
The price of silver in India is now about 250,000 rupees per kilogram, more than three times the level of a few years ago.
One shopkeeper said a pair that once cost about $125 now costs over $600, and he has sold nothing for three months.
Many craftsmen have left the trade, and some families now plan to pass old pairs down to new brides.
why: Silver prices rose sharply during the war with Iran, and India also raised its import taxes on silver in May.

stories.title: South African judge Navi Pillay wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
summary: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has given the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old judge from South Africa.
Pillay is a former UN human rights chief, and she has worked as a judge at the International Criminal Court and at a UN court for crimes in Rwanda.
The committee said her work had greatly widened the reach of international law.
It chose her from 287 nominations, and it had not yet spoken to her when it announced the prize in Oslo.
why: The committee said that ending conflicts without violence depends on countries following international law.

stories.title: The US puts sanctions on the International Criminal Court
summary: The United States has placed sanctions on the International Criminal Court as a whole, only hours after a former judge of the court won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would not allow the court to prosecute Americans.
Washington objects to the court's arrest warrants for Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The measures start in six months, and they could stop banks and other companies from working with the court.
why: The court has 125 member countries, and European Union leaders said they would act to keep it working.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres criticised the decision, while Netanyahu welcomed it.

stories.title: A strong earthquake shakes Panama and causes tsunami warnings
summary: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck near the southern coast of Panama on Friday morning, local time, according to the US Geological Survey.
Warnings of dangerous tsunami waves were issued for several countries on the Pacific coast, and people in Panama City ran out of buildings into the streets.
Damage was reported in central provinces, where a church fell down, but there were no early reports of deaths.
why: President José Raúl Mulino asked people to stay calm.
Several strong aftershocks followed the main earthquake.

stories.title: Houthi missile attack hits the main airport in Saudi Arabia's capital
summary: Yemen's Houthi group says it fired a ballistic missile at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
The national airline Saudia said one of its pilots was killed and one of its planes was damaged.
Saudi officials say attacks on the country's airports this week have killed three civilians and injured 36 people.
The airport reopened on Friday, and officials said flights were back to normal.
why: The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, have told airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
The war in Yemen had been mostly frozen for years, but fighting grew again after the US war on Iran began.

stories.title: AI company Firmus cancels Australia's biggest share sale in decades
summary: Firmus Technologies, a Sydney company that builds data centres for artificial intelligence, has cancelled its plan to list on the Australian stock exchange.
It wanted to raise about $7 billion at a value of $43.7 billion, which would have made it the biggest float since Telstra in 1997.
Some investors said the price was too high, while the company blamed unstable markets.
Chipmaker Nvidia owns 7.2 per cent of Firmus, which now plans to look for private funding and try to list on the Nasdaq next year.
why: The failed sale comes amid fears of an AI bubble, where company values rise much faster than their earnings.

stories.title: Police find two Renoir paintings stolen from a French museum
summary: Two paintings by the French artist Renoir have been found, and six people have been arrested, officials in southern France said on Friday.
The paintings, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well, were taken from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer last month.
The thieves cut through a fence and climbed in through a window, and the robbery lasted less than three minutes.
They took four paintings but left two of them behind as they escaped.
why: The town's mayor, Bryan Masson, said the paintings are part of the town's heritage.
The theft has led to new calls for better security at museums in France, a year after jewels were stolen from the Louvre in Paris.

stories.title: Birds return to an Australian reef island once destroyed by mining
summary: Lady Elliot Island, a small coral island at the southern end of the Great Barrier Reef, was stripped bare by guano mining more than 150 years ago.
Miners removed about 20,000 tonnes of guano, which is seabird droppings used as fertiliser, and the island stayed almost empty of plants for more than 100 years.
Families who ran tourism on the island have planted more than 20,000 trees, and the work is now about 70 per cent complete.
About 100,000 black noddies, a type of seabird, now nest there each year, up from only a few thousand about 60 years ago.
why: A researcher called it an extraordinary recovery, and it shows that damaged nature can come back with long-term care.

stories.title: A Russian strike on a bus stop in eastern Ukraine kills at least 33 people
summary: A Russian glide bomb hit two city buses at a bus stop in Kramatorsk, a city near the front line in eastern Ukraine, killing at least 33 people and wounding 18, according to Ukrainian officials.
City officials said there were no military targets nearby, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack would not go unanswered.
It came a day after a missile hit an apartment block in the northern town of Pryluky and killed 22 people.
why: Peace talks have stalled because Russia wants Ukraine to give up the rest of the Donetsk region, which Kyiv refuses to do.
The United Nations has confirmed more than 17,000 civilian deaths since 2022 and says the real number is much higher.

stories.title: Oil climbs above $100 as attacks on tankers revive fears for Gulf supplies
summary: Brent crude oil rose to about US$101 a barrel in early trading on Thursday after a rise in attacks on ships in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
On Wall Street, shares slipped from record highs, and US government bond yields climbed to their highest level in 24 years.
Investors worry that expensive oil will push up inflation and keep interest rates high.
why: A large share of the world's oil travels through the Strait of Hormuz, so even small disruptions can raise fuel prices everywhere.
Last week the G7 and the International Energy Agency agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel from reserves to calm the market.

stories.title: WHO presses Russia for answers after a fatal plague case in Siberia
summary: A 28-year-old woman who worked at a plague research institute in Irkutsk, Siberia, has died of what doctors suspect was pneumonic plague, the most dangerous form of the disease.
Russian media then reported a second worker with an unexplained pneumonia, but the Kremlin called most of the reports false and health officials said no staff were infected.
The World Health Organization has asked Russia for a formal response and says it still does not know the source of the infection.
why: Under international health rules, countries are expected to report quickly any outbreak that could spread to other countries.
Plague can be treated with antibiotics if it is found early.

stories.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
summary: Anne Carson, a 76-year-old poet and essayist from Toronto, has won this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.
The Swedish Academy praised her bold and inventive work, which plays with ancient Greek and Roman literature and mixes poetry, essay and fiction in new forms.
Her best-known books include Autobiography of Red, a novel written in verse, and the prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about US$1.7 million.
why: Carson was in Iceland when the news came and was very surprised, according to the Academy.
She is also known for her translations of ancient Greek poetry, including the work of Sappho.

stories.title: Japan's competition watchdog raids the country's four biggest beer makers
summary: Japan's Fair Trade Commission has raided Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory, which together sell about 90 per cent of the beer in Japan.
The watchdog is investigating whether the companies acted as a cartel by raising prices at the same time over several years, blaming costs such as raw materials.
All four brewers said they would cooperate, and shares in three of them fell nearly 4 per cent after the raids were reported.
why: Competition laws ban rival companies from agreeing on prices, because that can make customers pay more.
If the commission finds the law was broken, it can file a criminal complaint.

stories.title: Indonesians take their government to court over months of wildfire smoke
summary: Community groups in West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, have sued Indonesia's president, ministers and local leaders, saying the government failed to deal with peatland fires and the haze they create.
The fires began in July, and the Health Ministry has recorded at least 175,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to the smoke since August.
The groups want the fires declared a national emergency, free health care for vulnerable people, and those responsible to be prosecuted.
why: Smoke from Indonesian fires often drifts to Singapore and Malaysia, and burning peatland releases large amounts of carbon.
Police say they have named 196 suspects and are investigating 96 companies, but the rainy season is not expected in most areas until November.

stories.title: China gives AI 'digital humans' their own ID cards
summary: Beijing is testing a programme that gives identity cards to AI digital humans, the computer-made characters that appear in ads, videos and livestreams.
The first card went to a virtual pop idol called Yuri, and it records a name, birthday, address and facial features.
Supporters say registration will protect intellectual property and fight online scams, while critics warn it could expand state surveillance.
why: At least 1.3 million Chinese companies are linked to the digital human industry, which was worth about 48 billion yuan, or US$10 billion, in 2025.

stories.title: Taiwan moves toward restarting nuclear power as AI drives up electricity demand
summary: Taiwan's Nuclear Safety Commission has finished reviewing plans to restart the Maanshan nuclear power plant, which was shut down in May 2025.
If safety checks go well, the plant could produce power again as early as 2028, helping to meet rising demand from chip factories, data centres and artificial intelligence.
Taiwan imports about 96 per cent of its energy, and last year gas and coal produced more than 80 per cent of its electricity.
why: Taiwan turned away from nuclear power after Japan's Fukushima disaster in 2011, so a restart would be a major change in policy.
Critics say the plant is too small to make a big difference and that the problem of radioactive waste is still unsolved.
